body.statement:
Let \(\Phi(h)\) be the origin-constrained deterministic Brownian--GCM likelihood-ratio energy generated by \(t^2+h(t)\), and, for \(b>0\), let \(h_b(t)=b^2h(t/b)\). Whenever these energies are defined,
\[
 \Phi(h_b)=b^3\Phi(h).
\]
If \(h\) is absolutely continuous, \(h(0)=0\), and \(h'\in L^2(\mathbb R)\), then
\[
 \frac12\lVert h_b'\rVert_2^2=b^3\frac12\lVert h'\rVert_2^2.
\]
Consequently, for every \(u>0\),
\[
 \Pr\{D(0)>u\}=\Pr\{\Phi(u^{-1/2}\mathbb W)>1\}.
\]
For
\[
 I_\star=\inf\left\{\frac12\lVert h'\rVert_2^2:h(0)=0,\ h'\in L^2(\mathbb R),\ \Phi(h)\ge1\right\},
\]
one has the deterministic bracket
\[
 \frac12\le I_\star\le\frac98.
\]
The upper bound is attained as a witness value by \(k=4^{1/3}\), \(a=k/4\), and \(h'(t)=(k-2t)\mathbf 1\{-a\le t\le k/2\}\), for which \(\Phi(h)=1\) and \(\frac12\lVert h'\rVert_2^2=9/8\). No large-deviation limit or probability-tail rate is inferred from \(I_\star\).
body.justification: Provides exact scaling, a computable action bracket, and an explicit unit-energy witness.
body.gap: The infinite-domain LDP and every sharp cluster or extreme-value conclusion remain unproved.
body.consumer: The result guides future excursion analysis but supplies no critical value.
body.proof_tex:
For a deterministic perturbation \(h\), put \(F_h(t)=t^2+h(t)\).  If \(h_b(t)=b^2h(t/b)\) for \(b>0\), then
\[
 F_{h_b}(t)=b^2F_h(t/b). \tag{1}
\]
Let \(G_h\) be the unrestricted greatest convex minorant of \(F_h\).  The function \(t\mapsto b^2G_h(t/b)\) is convex and lies below the right-hand side of (1).  Conversely, applying the inverse dilation to any convex minorant of \(F_{h_b}\) produces a convex minorant of \(F_h\).  Maximality on both sides therefore gives
\[
 G_{h_b}(t)=b^2G_h(t/b). \tag{2}
\]
The same order-preserving argument on the left and right half-lines gives (2) for the origin-constrained minorants.  Hence every corresponding slope is multiplied by \(b\).  With the substitution \(t=bs\), the defining difference of squared-slope energies in \(\texttt{def:excursion-regime}\) becomes
\[
 \Phi(h_b)=b^3\Phi(h), \tag{3}
\]
whenever the two energies are defined.

If \(h\) is absolutely continuous, then \(h_b'(t)=b h'(t/b)\) for almost every \(t\).  The condition \(h'\in L^2(\mathbb R)\) and a change of variables give
\[
 \frac12\lVert h_b'\rVert_2^2
 =\frac12\int_{\mathbb R}b^2\{h'(t/b)\}^2\,dt
 =b^3\frac12\lVert h'\rVert_2^2. \tag{4}
\]

Fix \(u>0\), set \(b=u^{1/3}\), and set \(\epsilon=u^{-1/2}=b^{-3/2}\).  Brownian self-similarity, which follows by comparing the zero means and covariances of the two centered Gaussian processes, gives
\[
 b^{1/2}\mathbb W(\,\cdot\,/b)\stackrel{d}{=}\mathbb W.
\]
Moreover,
\[
 (\epsilon\mathbb W)_b(t)
 =b^2\epsilon\mathbb W(t/b)
 =b^{1/2}\mathbb W(t/b).
\]
Using the fixed-location well-posedness from \(\texttt{lem:canonical-wellposedness}\), the identity \(D(0)=\Phi(\mathbb W)\) from \(\texttt{def:canonical-field}\), and (3), we obtain
\[
 D(0)\stackrel{d}{=}\Phi((\epsilon\mathbb W)_b)
 =b^3\Phi(\epsilon\mathbb W)
 =u\Phi(u^{-1/2}\mathbb W).
\]
Therefore
\[
 \Pr\{D(0)>u\}=\Pr\{\Phi(u^{-1/2}\mathbb W)>1\}. \tag{5}
\]

We next establish the lower action bound without interpreting it as a probability-tail rate.  Let \(h(0)=0\), let \(h'\in L^2(\mathbb R)\), and write
\[
 y(t)=2t+h'(t).
\]
On a finite interval, let \(g\) denote the unrestricted GCM slope of a primitive of \(y\).  If \(G\) is that GCM and \(H=F_h-G\), then \(H\ge0\), the positive measure \(dg\) is carried by the contact set \(\{H=0\}\), and \(H\) vanishes at the relevant endpoints.  For every nondecreasing slope competitor \(v\), integration by parts gives
\[
 \int (y-g)(v-g)
 =-\int H\,dv+\int H\,dg
 \le0. \tag{6}
\]
On the two half-intervals the same calculation applies to the constrained slope \(g^0\); the possible boundary term at the split has nonpositive sign because the left slope is capped at zero and the right slope is floored at zero.  Thus (6) is also the variational inequality for the origin-constrained cone.  Both slope classes are convex cones.  Taking successively the competitors \(0\) and \(2g\), and then \(0\) and \(2g^0\), in their respective inequalities yields
\[
 \int (y-g)g=0,
 \qquad
 \int (y-g^0)g^0=0. \tag{7}
\]
Expanding squares and using (7) shows that the constrained-versus-unconstrained residual sum-of-squares difference equals the likelihood-ratio energy:
\[
 \int\{(y-g^0)^2-(y-g)^2\}
 =\int\{g^2-(g^0)^2\}. \tag{8}
\]
The linear slope \(\ell(t)=2t\) is nondecreasing and satisfies the origin split constraint.  Hence least-squares optimality of \(g^0\), nonnegativity of squared loss, and (8) imply on every finite interval
\[
 0\le \Phi(h)
 \le \int\{y(t)-\ell(t)\}^2\,dt
 =\int\{h'(t)\}^2\,dt. \tag{9}
\]
For an infinite-domain energy, apply the preceding argument on an increasing sequence of finite contact intervals.  The defining GCM energies are the corresponding exhaustion limits whenever \(\Phi(h)\) is well defined, while the right side increases to \(\lVert h'\rVert_2^2\).  Thus (9) remains valid on \(\mathbb R\).  In particular, \(\Phi(h)\ge1\) implies
\[
 \frac12\lVert h'\rVert_2^2\ge\frac12.
\]
Taking the infimum in \(\texttt{def:excursion-regime}\) proves
\[
 I_\star\ge\frac12. \tag{10}
\]

For the upper bound, let \(k=4^{1/3}\), let \(a=k/4\), and define the absolutely continuous perturbation by \(h(0)=0\) and
\[
 h'(t)=(k-2t)\mathbf 1\{-a\le t\le k/2\}. \tag{11}
\]
This derivative has compact support and is square integrable.  The derivative of \(F_h\) is
\[
 y(t)=2t+h'(t)=
 \begin{cases}
 2t,&t<-a,\\
 k,&-a\le t\le k/2,\\
 2t,&t>k/2.
 \end{cases} \tag{12}
\]
Since \(-2a=-k/2<k\) and \(2(k/2)=k\), the function in (12) is nondecreasing.  Thus \(F_h\) is convex and its unrestricted GCM slope is \(y\).  By the cap-and-floor construction in \(\texttt{def:canonical-field}\), the origin-constrained slope is
\[
 g^0(t)=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&-a\le t\le0,\\
 y(t),&t\notin[-a,0].
 \end{cases} \tag{13}
\]
Indeed, to the left of the origin the only portion of the unrestricted slope exceeding zero is the plateau in (12), and to the right it is already bounded below by zero.  Equations (12)--(13) therefore give
\[
 \Phi(h)=\int_{-a}^{0}k^2\,dt=ak^2=\frac{k^3}{4}=1. \tag{14}
\]
The action of this perturbation is
\[
 \frac12\lVert h'\rVert_2^2
 =\frac12\int_{-a}^{k/2}(k-2t)^2\,dt
 =\frac{(k+2a)^3}{12}
 =\frac{(3k/2)^3}{12}
 =\frac98. \tag{15}
\]
Thus the witness is admissible for the action problem and proves \(I_\star\le9/8\).

For clarity about maximality, the same calculation for the full one-plateau family with arbitrary \(k,a>0\) gives \(\Phi(h)=ak^2\).  Under the unit-energy restriction \(ak^2=1\), put \(r=2a/k>0\).  Then \(k^3=2/r\), and the action is
\[
 \frac{(k+2a)^3}{12}=\frac{(1+r)^3}{6r}. \tag{16}
\]
Its derivative has the sign of \(2r-1\), so (16) is minimized at \(r=1/2\), where it equals \(9/8\).  Hence (11) is optimal within this one-plateau family, but (10) and (15) give only the global bracket
\[
 \frac12\le I_\star\le\frac98.
\]
Neither the bracket, the within-family optimization, nor the exact scaling identity supplies an infinite-domain large-deviation principle, a sharp tail rate, a Palm intensity, or an extreme-value limit.
